translations.text: A king must rule a kingdom. Cities can be seen from far away, the skilful work of giants, those that are on this earth, the wondrous work of wall-stones.
Wind is the swiftest thing in the air; thunder is at times the loudest. The glories of Christ are great; fate is strongest.

Winter is coldest, spring frostiest (it stays cold longest), summer brightest with sunshine (the sun is hottest then), autumn most gloriously blessed: it brings to men the year's fruits, which God sends them.
Truth is most evident; treasure is most precious, gold, to every man; and an old man is wisest, made wise by the years gone by, he who has lived through much before.
Wax is wondrously sticky. Clouds glide.
Good companions must urge a young prince on to battle and to the giving of rings.

Courage must be in a nobleman; the blade must meet battle against the helmet. The hawk must stay wild on the glove; the wolf must be in the grove, the wretched loner; the boar must be in the wood, strong in the might of its tusks.

The good man must win glory in his homeland. The javelin must be in the hand, the spear adorned with gold. The gem must stand in the ring, high and broad. The stream must mingle in the waves with the sea-flood.
The mast must be on the ship, and the sail-yard must hang from it. The sword must be in the lap, the lordly iron. The dragon must be in the burial mound, old and proud of its treasures.
The fish must breed its kind in the water. The king must give out rings in the hall. The bear must be on the heath, old and terrible. The river must run down from the hill, flood-grey.
An army must stand together, a troop of glorious men. Loyalty must be in a nobleman, wisdom in a man. The wood must bloom with leaves on the earth. The hill must stand green on the earth.
God must be in the heavens, the judge of deeds. A door must be on the hall, the wide mouth of the building. The boss must be on the shield, the firm protection of the fingers.
The bird must sport aloft in the air. The salmon must glide in the pool with the trout. The shower must come from the heavens, mixed with wind, into this world.

The thief must go about in dark weather. The giant must live in the fen, alone in the land. A woman, a maiden, must seek her lover by secret craft, if she does not wish to marry properly among the people, so that a man buys her with rings.
The sea must surge with salt; the cloud-covering and the ocean flood must flow around every land, the mighty streams.
Cattle must breed and bear young on the earth. A star must shine brightly in the heavens, as the Creator commanded it.

Good must fight against evil, youth against age, life against death, light against darkness, army against army, enemy against enemy, foe against foe; they must contend over land and charge each other with wrongs.
The wise man must always think about the strife of this world. The criminal must hang and duly pay for the crime he once committed against mankind.
The Lord alone knows where the soul must go afterwards, and all the spirits that go before God after their death-day and await judgement in the Father's embrace.

The future state is hidden and secret; only the Lord knows it, the saving Father. No one comes back here under our roofs who could truly tell people what the Creator's creation is like, the dwellings of the victorious peoples where he himself lives.
